title: Unlocking Cures for Pediatric Cancer With Artificial Intelligence
summary:
The White House issued an order to speed up progress against childhood cancer by using artificial intelligence to improve data, research, and patient care. The goal is faster diagnoses, better treatments, and more effective clinical trials, all while protecting families’ privacy.

The plan builds on a national effort to collect and share childhood cancer data. It directs the administration’s health commission, working with the Department of Health and Human Services and science advisors, to push new projects at National Cancer Institute–designated centers. Priorities include bringing together data from many sources so it’s ready for analysis, using advanced tools to predict how a child might respond to treatment or experience side effects, and designing clinical trials that are easier to join and more informative. The government will look to increase support from existing funds and encourage companies to bring their best technology to this work. The Department of Health and Human Services is also asked to set clear, safe standards so medical records and insurance data can be used in research and trial design, with parents and patients keeping control over their information.

Children and teens with cancer, along with their families, stand to benefit most if this leads to earlier detection, more personalized care, and better access to trials. Doctors and researchers could gain stronger tools and richer data, helping them learn faster and share what works. Hospitals and research centers may improve care pathways, and health technology companies could find new opportunities to build trusted, life‑saving tools.

There are also risks and trade‑offs. Sharing more data, even with safeguards, raises privacy and security concerns. Smaller clinics may face costs to upgrade systems and meet new standards. If the technology is not carefully tested, it could deepen disparities or miss key needs in rural and underrepresented communities. Some fear other health priorities could receive less attention if resources shift. The order itself doesn’t create new rights and depends on existing budgets and laws. Its impact will come down to careful rollout, strong protections, and close collaboration among government, researchers, industry, and families.
